narr: Welcome to Week 7 of our quantitative reasoning journey. This week, we're learning how to reason when data are scarce, and how to read the same numbers in more than one way.
First, let's recap what we covered in Week 6 in one breath: demand and capacity, intensities and flows, estimation techniques, and bounding methods.

data.heading: Key Statements of Week 7
bullets: Reason when data are scarce
Read the same numbers in more than one way
Demand and capacity — what is asked against what can be delivered
Intensities and flows — amount per unit of time
Power × time = energy
Change = inflow − outflow
Estimation — break into factors, round to one digit, check units
Bounding — low, typical, high, and stop when decision no longer changes

narr: In Week 7, we'll focus on several key concepts that will help us make better decisions with limited information.

data.heading: Five Ways Data Can Be Incomplete
bullets: Too little — Only a few points
Missing — No data for the case we care about
Noisy — Values scatter around the truth
Outdated/unrepresentative — Measured under other conditions
Wrong definition or unit — The quantity is not what we think

narr: The week's hook presents us with three test trips showing energy consumption of 1.1, 1.3, and 1.6 kWh/km. Which number should we use for the range promise?
Before choosing a number, we need to name the data problem. There are five ways data can be incomplete.

bullets: Measure — High trust if method is stated

data.heading: Ranges Instead of Single Numbers
bullets: Three summer trips give consumption of 1.1, 1.3, 1.6 kWh/km
All cases cover daily requirement of 96 km
High-consumption case has only 4 km margin
Report: "about 100 to 145 km"

narr: Instead of using a single number, we should often use ranges. Three summer trips give us consumption values of 1.1, 1.3, and 1.6 kWh/km.
Calculating the range from a 160 kWh battery gives us 145, 123/100 kilometers. All three cases cover the daily requirement of 96 km, but the high-consumption case only has a 4 km margin.
When reporting, we should say "about 100 to 145 km" to communicate the uncertainty in our data. A range tells the reader how far to trust the answer.
Here's the formula for calculating the range. R equals the total energy available divided by the energy consumption per kilometer.
With consumption values of 1.1, 1.3, and 1.6 kWh/km, we get ranges of approximately 145, 123/100 kilometers respectively.

data.heading: Small Samples: State n
bullets: Three trips: mean = (1.1 + 1.3 + 1.6) ÷ 3 = 1.33 kWh/km
One odd trip moves the mean a lot
Median = 1.3 kWh/km — the middle element in order
One odd trip barely moves the median
Sample size n = 3 — write n next to every number you report
With three points, give a range and n; don't claim more than three trips can show

narr: When working with small samples, we need to be careful about how we report our findings. With only three trips, the mean is (1.1 + 1.3 + 1.6) ÷ 3 = 1.33 kWh/km.
Notice how one odd trip can move the mean value significantly. The median, however, is 1.3 kWh/km — the middle element when ordered, which one odd trip barely affects.

Crucially, we must state our sample size n next to every number we report. With only three data points, we should give a range and n, and never claim that three trips can show more than they actually can.
Here's the calculation for both mean and median with our three data points. Notice how the mean is affected more by the outlier value than the median.
Always remember to report your sample size n, as it tells readers how much confidence they should have in your statistics.

data.heading: Triangulation: Estimate in Three Ways
bullets: Triangulation is estimating one quantity by several independent routes
Example: faculty building consumption in kWh/day
Route 1: floor area × typical consumption = 8,000 m² × 0.35 kWh/m²·day ≈ 2,800
Route 2: load profile = 94 kW × 24 h ≈ 2,260
Route 3: monthly bill = 70,000 kWh/month ÷ 30 ≈ 2,330
Three independent routes agree to within about 25%

narr: Triangulation is a powerful technique where we estimate one quantity by several independent routes and compare the results.
Let's consider estimating the consumption of a faculty building in kWh/day. We can approach this in three different ways:
First, we can multiply the floor area by typical consumption: 8,000 square meters times 0.35 kWh per square meter per day gives approximately 2,800 kWh/day.
Second, we can use the load profile from lecture 6: 94 kW multiplied by 24 hours gives approximately 2,260 kWh/day.
Third, we can look at the monthly bill: 70,000 kWh per month divided by 30 gives approximately 2,330 kWh/day.
These three independent routes agree to within about 25%. Agreement builds trust in our estimate, while disagreement points us to where we should look for more information.
Here are the three calculations for triangulating the building's energy consumption. Notice how all three methods give us values that are reasonably close to each other.
When independent methods give similar results, we can be more confident in our estimate.

data.heading: One Dataset — Different Readings
bullets: Distribution of waiting times at a stop: 14, 26, 22, 12, 7, 4, 8, 7%
Dispatcher: "The average wait is 6 minutes. Good."
Passenger: "Every seventh of us waits more than 12 minutes" (≈15%)
Administrator: "Cutting the long waits requires more buses. What does that cost?"
One set of numbers, three readings — all three are true

narr: A single dataset can be read in multiple ways, and all readings can be true depending on your perspective.
Consider the distribution of waiting times at a bus stop: 14%, 26%, 22%, 12%, 7%, 4%, 8%, 7% of passengers wait in different time intervals.
The dispatcher might say: "The average wait is 6 minutes. Good." This is the mean waiting time.
A passenger might say: "Every seventh of us waits more than 12 minutes." This refers to the upper tail of the distribution.
The administrator might ask: "Cutting the long waits requires more buses. What does that cost?" This focuses on the worst cases.
All three perspectives are valid and true, but they emphasize different aspects of the same data.

rows.text: How long does the typical passenger wait?
How bad is it for the unlucky?

narr: The decision you're trying to make should choose the metric, not the other way around. Different metrics answer different questions.
If you want to know how long the typical passenger waits, you should look at the median, which is about 5 minutes.
If you want to know how much waiting time there is in total, you need the mean multiplied by the number of passengers.
If you're concerned about the unlucky passengers, you should look at the 90th percentile, which is about 13 minutes.
And if you're planning for the worst case, you need the maximum value, which is about 16 minutes.

data.heading: The Decision Chooses the Metric
bullets: The decision chooses the metric, not the other way round
Different metrics answer different questions
kWh answers "how much?"
kW answers "how fast?"
Choose the metric that serves your decision

narr: Remember that the decision you're trying to make should choose the metric, not the other way around.
As we saw in lecture 6, kWh answers "how much?" while kW answers "how fast?" The choice of metric depends on what question you're trying to answer.
Always choose the metric that serves your decision best, rather than forcing your decision to fit the metric you have.
